newsitem.title: USA: US stocks seen firm at open on book-to-bill boost.
newsitem.headline: US stocks seen firm at open on book-to-bill boost.

text.p: Technology shares are expected to lead Wall Street stocks higher at the open on Wednesday, but analysts said continued profit-taking could keep the Dow in check, further postponing a close over the 6000 mark.
The Semiconductor Industry Association said late Tuesday that its key indicator, the North America book-to-bill ratio, rose to 0.99 in September from 0.93 in August.
The reading beat estimates, which had averaged about 0.95, and showed continued improvement in the chip industry, which has undergone a sharp marketwide correction.
"The good news is that the book-to-bill came in on the strong side, showing that there is light at the end of the tunnel," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
Among chip shares, Intel Corp and Micron Technology Inc have already posted gains on the book-to-bill news, rising in after-hours activity on Tuesday.
Analysts noted that higher expectations are already reflected in shares in the sector, which might serve to cap any gains today.
"It will be helpful but remember, the semiconductors have had a long run up ahead of the book-to-bill," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities.
Wachtel said profit-taking would likely once again erode any sharp gains in the market, particularly in the Dow, which has rebounded ferociously from its July selloff.
"The market's problem is it's in an overbought condition, the Dow specifically," he said, adding that the 600-plus points in gains posted since the July lows "have to be rationalized by time."
Alone on the day's economic calendar is the 1000 EDT/1400 GMT scheduled release of August wholesale inventories. The report is not expected to be a major factor for markets.
In Tokyo, stocks were lower as investors remained wary ahead of general elections. The Nikkei 225 index fell 168 points to close at 28,871.
In London, U.S. stocks were steady to higher, with technology issues showing the most strength. The FTSE-100 fell 13 points to 4022.
The dollar was weak in Tokyo but managed to hold above 111 yen. In Europe, the dollar hovered around 1.53 marks.
Bonds were firm. The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury rose 11/32 to yield 6.78 percent.
The December S&P 500 index future rose 1.5 points to 706.25.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column focuses a California ballot initiative, Proposition 211, which is intended to protect investors from misleading statements by companies and their underwriters. Recently, Intel Corp said it would no longer discuss its prospects for fear of being sued under the rules, should voters pass the proposal.

The New York Times Marketplace column examines the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's plans to revise Regulation S, which allows U.S. companies to sell securities overseas. The rule has led to much abuse, the column states.
